findings.summary: Sparse section arrays can satisfy the top-level type guard.
findings.consequence: A non-JSON caller can pass an array with the required length but missing elements; `Array.prototype.every` skips holes, so the guard can return true for a value that is not an `AuthorWorksResponse`.
findings.evidence: The guard checks `value.authored_sections.length === authoredSections.length` and then validates sections via `value.authored_sections.every(...)` on line 368. JavaScript `every` does not invoke the callback for unassigned indexes, and the listed unit tests cover missing sections by `pop()` but not sparse arrays.
findings.recommendation: Iterate over the expected section descriptors instead, e.g. `authoredSections.every((expected, index) => isSection(value.authored_sections[index], expected.kind, expected.label, expected.showAuthor))`, so missing indexes are passed to `isSection` and rejected.
verification: Inspected `app/lib/author-works.ts` owned lines 358-386 and surrounding helper dependencies.

findings.summary: Sparse about-section arrays can satisfy the top-level type guard.
findings.consequence: A non-JSON caller can pass an `about_sections` array with four holes; `every` skips the missing section objects and the guard can accept a response shape that consumers and generated types expect to contain concrete section objects.
findings.evidence: The guard checks `value.about_sections.length === aboutSections.length` and then uses `value.about_sections.every(...)` on line 378. The callback is never run for array holes, and the named unit tests do not exercise sparse `about_sections`.
findings.recommendation: Validate from the expected descriptor list, e.g. `aboutSections.every((expected, index) => isSection(value.about_sections[index], expected.kind, expected.label(authorName), true))`, or first reject sparse arrays with an own-index check.
verification: Inspected `app/lib/author-works.ts` owned lines 358-386 and surrounding helper dependencies.
